conversation-designer.title: Script one short chatbot conversation
conversation-designer.need: A text editor or paper, and someone to read it aloud with if you can.

steps.text: Pick one thing a person might ask a chatbot for help with, such as changing a delivery slot.
Write the smooth version as a script of four to six turns, in plain words.
Add what happens when the person says something unexpected or the bot does not understand.
Read both versions aloud, in two voices. Mark every line that sounds clunky.
Rewrite the three clunkiest lines. Write three lines on what you changed and why.

conversation-designer.good: Someone could follow your script and finish the task without help, and the bot never blames the person.
conversation-designer.next: Script a second task, then keep both as portfolio pieces.

product-manager.title: Write a one-page product brief
product-manager.need: A text editor and one product you use that has an annoying flaw.

steps.text: Pick the product and the flaw. Describe who it affects.
Write the problem in one paragraph. List three pieces of evidence you could gather to check it is real.
List three possible fixes. Pick one and say what you give up by choosing it.
Decide how you would know it worked. Pick one number and say when you would check it.
Write what you would ship first in a week and what you would leave out.

product-manager.good: A colleague could read it in two minutes and say what you would build and why.
product-manager.next: Write a second brief for a different product, then read three live product manager job ads and note the overlap.

product-marketing-manager.title: Position one product
product-marketing-manager.need: A text editor and one product you know well.

steps.text: Pick the product and write who you think it is for.
Read what three competing products say on their home pages. Write down each promise.
Write one sentence of positioning: who it is for, what it does and why it beats the alternative.
Draft a short launch message for two different audiences.
Note which claims you would need evidence for before you published them.

product-marketing-manager.good: Someone outside the product could say who it is for and why it is different after one read.
product-marketing-manager.next: Do the same for a second product, then read three live product marketing job ads.

service-designer.title: Map one service from the customer's side
service-designer.need: Paper or a whiteboard, and a service you used recently that had several steps.

steps.text: Pick the service, such as renewing a document or registering with a doctor.
List every step, including the ones you could not see, such as calls, letters and waits.
Mark where the person felt unsure or waited. Put a number on how long.
For each pain point, note what staff, rules or systems behind the scenes cause it.
Sketch one change and say which part of the behind-the-scenes work it needs.

service-designer.good: Someone who works in that service would recognise your map and learn something from it.
service-designer.next: Map a second service, then read three live service designer job ads.

delivery-project-manager.title: Plan a small project
delivery-project-manager.need: A spreadsheet or paper, and a real small project such as a house move or a family event.

steps.text: Pick the project and write the date it must finish.
List every task and who owns each one.
Put the tasks in order, mark what depends on what, and estimate how long each takes.
List the five biggest risks and a first response to each.
Write a one-page status update for someone who has two minutes.

delivery-project-manager.good: Someone could take over the project from your plan without asking you anything.
delivery-project-manager.next: Plan a second project with more people involved, then read three live delivery manager job ads.

ux-researcher.title: Run two short interviews
ux-researcher.need: A notebook, two willing people and a product they both use.

steps.text: Pick a product or service and write what you want to learn about it.
Write five open questions that do not suggest an answer.
Interview two people for about 15 minutes each. Take notes on what they say and do, not on what you think.
Group your notes into themes.
Write three findings and one recommendation, each backed by something a person said.

ux-researcher.good: Every finding points to a real quote or action, and none relies on your own assumption.
ux-researcher.next: Run two more interviews with a different kind of person and compare what changes.

data-analyst.title: Find one story in a small dataset
data-analyst.need: A spreadsheet and a small table of your own data, such as a month of spending or bills.

steps.text: Pick the data and write three questions you want it to answer.
Clean it: fix dates, remove duplicates and fill obvious gaps.
Answer each question with a sum, an average or a chart.
Make one clear chart with a title that states the finding.
Write three sentences: what you found, how sure you are and what you would check next.

data-analyst.good: Someone could read your chart title and know the finding without reading anything else.
data-analyst.next: Repeat with a second dataset, then read three live data analyst job ads and note the tools they ask for.

business-analyst.title: Write requirements for a small change
business-analyst.need: A text editor and a process that frustrates you, such as a school form or a club sign-up.

steps.text: Pick the process and write who uses it.
Write how it works today as a list of steps.
Talk to one person who uses it and ask what they need.
Write five requirements as: As a (person), I need (something) so that (reason). Add a test for each.
List what is still unclear and who could answer.

business-analyst.good: Someone could build the change from your requirements and you could tell if it passed each test.
business-analyst.next: Write requirements for a second process, then read three live business analyst job ads.

content-designer.title: Rewrite one screen
content-designer.need: A text editor and one real page that confused you recently, such as a bank letter or a council web page.

steps.text: Pick the page and write in one sentence what a person is trying to get done on it.
Underline every word or sentence that slows that person down. Note who the reader is and what they already know.
Rewrite the first screen. Put the answer first, use short sentences and plain words, and give each button a clear label.
Read it aloud, then cut a third of the words. Check that nothing a person needs has gone.
Write three lines on what you changed and why. This becomes your first portfolio piece.

content-designer.good: Someone who has never seen the page could do the task from your version alone.
content-designer.next: Rewrite a second page, then read three live content designer job ads.

accessibility-specialist.title: Check one page for barriers
accessibility-specialist.need: A laptop and one page you use often. Use the screen reader built into your device.

steps.text: Pick the page and one task a person must complete on it.
Use only the keyboard. Note whether you can reach everything and always see where you are.
Zoom to 200 percent and use a free colour contrast checker on three pieces of text.
Turn on the screen reader and listen to the first screen. Note anything confusing or missing.
Write the three biggest barriers, who each one affects and how you would fix it.

accessibility-specialist.good: Each barrier names a real person it blocks and a fix a developer could act on.
accessibility-specialist.next: Check a second page, then read three live accessibility specialist job ads.

front-end-developer.title: Build one small page
front-end-developer.need: A code editor, a browser and a small subject such as a recipe card or a short bio.

steps.text: Pick what the page is and sketch it on paper.
Write the HTML first, with no styling, so the page makes sense on its own.
Add CSS for layout, type and colour.
Make it work at phone width.
Check it with the keyboard and at 200 percent zoom. Write down what you would tidy.

front-end-developer.good: The page opens in a browser, reads well on a phone and works with the keyboard.
front-end-developer.next: Build a second page that uses a little JavaScript, then read three live front-end developer job ads.

technical-writer.title: Write a how-to
technical-writer.need: A text editor and something you know how to do, such as setting up a router.

steps.text: Pick the task and write who the reader is and what they already know.
List the steps in rough order.
Write them as numbered steps with one action each and what the person should see afterwards.
Ask someone to follow it without your help. Note where they stall.
Fix the three worst steps.

technical-writer.good: A stranger could finish the task using only your words.
technical-writer.next: Write a how-to for something more technical, then read three live technical writer job ads.

customer-success-manager.title: Plan a customer's first 30 days
customer-success-manager.need: A text editor and a product you use. Imagine you are looking after a new customer of it.

steps.text: Pick the product and write who the new customer is.
Write what a happy customer should be able to do after 30 days.
Draft a welcome message and a check-in message for day 7.
List three warning signs that a customer is struggling and what you would say for each.
Write a short, kind note to a customer who wants to cancel.

customer-success-manager.good: Your messages sound like a helpful person and give the customer one clear next thing to do.
customer-success-manager.next: Plan the first 30 days for a different kind of customer, then read three live customer success manager job ads.

learning-experience-designer.title: Design a 20-minute lesson
learning-experience-designer.need: A text editor and one skill you could teach someone, such as changing a bike tyre.

steps.text: Pick the skill and the learner.
Write one learning goal: after this, the person can do (something).
Outline three activities and a short check at the end.
Write the first activity in full, with instructions.
Ask someone to try it. Note where they were confused.

learning-experience-designer.good: The learner can do the thing at the end, and you can tell from the check, not from how they say they felt.
learning-experience-designer.next: Build a second lesson, then read three live learning experience designer job ads.
